# Compliance Requirements for High-Risk AI Hiring Tools Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
AI-powered hiring tools—resume screening, candidate ranking, interview automation, and employment-decision systems—are widely described as falling under Annex III of the EU AI Act as high-risk systems, though this classification claim itself carries only low confidence based on available sourcing (low confidence) [HeyMilo](https://www.heymilo.ai/blog/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know), [Merified](https://www.merified.com/resources/eu-ai-act-guide). By contrast, the resulting deployer and provider obligations that attach to high-risk status are well-documented and rated high confidence (high confidence) [Regulation AI](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/annex-iii), [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3). The compliance timeline has also shifted: the Digital Omnibus agreement has deferred standalone Annex III obligations, including recruitment tools, from August 2026 to December 2, 2027 (high confidence) [Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass). No source in this research identifies any actual enforcement action, fine, or investigation targeting a company's AI hiring tool to date.

## Key Findings

### Classification as High-Risk
AI systems used for recruitment—including resume screening, candidate ranking, AI interview agents, performance evaluation, promotion, task allocation, and termination decisions—are described by industry sources as falling under Annex III, Section 4 as high-risk AI systems, though this specific claim is rated low confidence given weak sourcing authority (low confidence) [HeyMilo](https://www.heymilo.ai/blog/how-the-eu-ai-act-changes-recruitment-and-what-employers-need-to-know), [Merified](https://www.merified.com/resources/eu-ai-act-guide). A narrow derogation under Article 6(3) allows exemption if the system performs a limited procedural task without significant risk of harm, but this exemption does not apply where the system profiles natural persons—a condition many hiring tools likely meet, effectively excluding them from the derogation (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-6).

### Deployer Obligations
Companies deploying high-risk hiring AI must use the system according to provider instructions, implement human oversight, monitor performance, report serious incidents, inform workers or their representatives when AI affects employment decisions, and avoid using the system beyond its intended purpose (high confidence) [Regulation AI](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/annex-iii), [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-provider-deployer-obligations). Deployers must also satisfy Article 4 AI literacy obligations, which remain in force independent of the Annex III deadline extension (medium confidence) [Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass). Certain deployers—public bodies, private entities providing public services, and users of specific Annex III systems—must complete a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) under Article 27 before first use (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-27).

### Provider Obligations
Providers bear extensive pre-market duties under Articles 8–15, including risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency disclosures to deployers, human-oversight design, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity assurance (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3), [Modulos](https://docs.modulos.ai/frameworks/eu-ai-act/high-risk-ai-systems).

### Timeline
The original Annex III compliance deadline was August 2, 2026 (low confidence) [Warden AI](https://www.warden-ai.com/resources/eu-ai-act-hiring-recruitment), but the Digital Omnibus has deferred this to December 2, 2027 for standalone systems like recruitment tools (high confidence) [Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/en/apply-ai-alliance/community-content/eu-ai-act-and-recruitment-why-december-2027-extension-prep-window-not-free-pass), [Regulation AI](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/annex-iii). AI embedded in regulated products faces a separate August 2028 deadline (low confidence) [Axipro](https://axipro.co/eu-ai-act-recruitment-tools). GPAI model obligations took effect from August 2026 regardless (high confidence) [European Commission](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai).

### Enforcement
From August 2, 2026, the Commission's AI Office and national authorities began enforcing AI Act rules alongside new transparency requirements (medium confidence) [European Commission](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-starts-enforcing-ai-act-rules-and-new-transparency-requirements-2-august). National Market Surveillance Authorities conduct most compliance investigations (low confidence) [Orrick](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2024/09/The-EU-AI-Act-Oversight-and-Enforcement). Penalties for high-risk non-compliance can reach €15 million or 3% of global turnover (low confidence) [Orbiq](https://www.orbiqhq.com/eu-regulations/eu-ai-act-compliance), while supplying misleading information carries fines up to €7.5 million or 1% of turnover (high confidence) [European Commission](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/enforcement-ai-act).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on whether Parliament or Council gave final approval for the Digital Omnibus deferral [Warden AI](https://www.warden-ai.com/resources/eu-ai-act-hiring-recruitment) vs. [Axipro](https://axipro.co/eu-ai-act-recruitment-tools), both **low confidence**. Official EU Commission announcements of an August 2026 enforcement start date do not clearly reconcile with the December 2027 Annex III deferral, leaving ambiguity about what obligations apply to hiring-tool deployers in the interim [Axipro](https://axipro.co/eu-ai-act-recruitment-tools) vs. [European Commission](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/european-approach-artificial-intelligence). Several timeline and penalty claims rate **low confidence** (0.10–0.20), including the specific Council approval date of June 29, 2026, the August 2025 penalty applicability claim, and—notably—the core claim that hiring tools fall under Annex III Section 4, which should all be treated cautiously pending primary legal text verification.

## Knowledge Gaps
No evidence confirms any enforcement action, fine, or investigation against a hiring-tool deployer to date. The legislative status of the Digital Omnibus deferral (final vs. pending) is unclear. It remains unresolved whether private-sector recruitment deployers must conduct FRIAs under Article 27, and how Article 6(3)'s narrow-risk derogation applies practically to profiling-based hiring tools. Additionally, the underlying classification of hiring tools as Annex III high-risk systems rests on lower-authority industry sources rather than definitive primary legal text, warranting further verification.

report:
# EU AI Act Foundation Model Requirements vs. US Federal AI Policy: A Comparative Analysis

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act imposes binding, detailed legal obligations on general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers—including documentation, copyright compliance, and training data transparency—reportedly overseen by a centralized AI Office and, according to lower-confidence sources, backed by significant financial penalties ([EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/general-purpose-ai-models-ai-act-questions-answers), [Glocert](https://www.glocertinternational.com/resources/guides/eu-ai-act-gpai-and-foundation-model-compliance)). By contrast, current US federal AI policy lacks comparable binding legislation, relying instead on executive orders and voluntary frameworks like NIST's AI RMF, creating a substantial regulatory asymmetry between the two jurisdictions ([Oliver Patel](https://oliverpatel.substack.com/p/us-ai-law-and-policy-explained), [Trustible](https://trustible.ai/ai-governance-frameworks-nist-ai-rmf-eu-ai-act-iso-42001-compared)).

## Key Findings

### EU AI Act Requirements for GPAI Providers
Article 53 of the AI Act requires GPAI model providers to maintain technical documentation, share information with downstream providers, and implement a policy ensuring compliance with EU copyright law, including honoring text-and-data-mining opt-out reservations (high confidence) ([Clifford Chance](https://www.cliffordchance.com/insights/resources/blogs/ip-insights/2025/10/copyright-compliance-under-the-eu-ai-act-for-gpai-model-providers.html), [EU Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/general-purpose-ai-models-ai-act-questions-answers)). Providers must also publish a "sufficiently detailed summary" of training data content (high confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/774095/IUST_STU(2025)774095_EN.pdf)). Providers of free and open-source GPAI models receive lighter obligations under Article 53(2), exempting them from some documentation and transparency duties unless the model poses systemic risk (medium confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/778575/ECTI_STU(2025)778575_EN.pdf)). A model is deemed to present "systemic risk" if it has high-impact capabilities or significant Union market reach, per Recitals 110–111 (high confidence) ([JRC](https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/bitstream/JRC143260/JRC143260_01.pdf)).

Lower-confidence sources add further structural and enforcement detail that should be treated with caution: one source describes Chapter V (Articles 53–55) as the section setting out GPAI obligations with extra duties for systemic-risk models (low confidence) ([Prighter](https://prighter.com/tr/resources/ai-act-obligations-for-general-purpose-ai-models)); another states the AI Office holds exclusive enforcement competence distinct from national authorities (low confidence) ([Glocert](https://www.glocertinternational.com/resources/guides/eu-ai-act-gpai-and-foundation-model-compliance)); and others report GPAI-related fines reaching 3% of global turnover or €15 million, with prohibited-practice violations under Article 5 reaching up to 7% of turnover or €35 million (low confidence) ([Glocert](https://www.glocertinternational.com/resources/guides/eu-ai-act-gpai-and-foundation-model-compliance), [Modulos](https://docs.modulos.ai/frameworks/comparison/nist-ai-rmf-vs-eu-ai-act)). Reported compliance timelines (obligations effective August 2025, enforcement from August 2026, legacy models compliant by August 2027) are drawn from a single low-confidence source and should be treated cautiously ([ECCouncil](https://www.eccouncil.org/cybersecurity-exchange/responsible-ai-governance/eu-ai-act-nist-ai-rmf-and-iso-iec-42001-a-plain-english-comparison)).

### US Federal Approach
There is no comprehensive federal AI law in the US comparable to the AI Act; federal action instead comprises scattered measures like export controls and infrastructure funding (low confidence) ([Oliver Patel](https://oliverpatel.substack.com/p/us-ai-law-and-policy-explained)). Current policy rests on two Trump-era executive orders—EO 14179 (January 2025) and EO 14365 (December 2025)—neither of which is congressional law nor directly regulates company conduct (low confidence) ([CASRAI](https://casrai.org/guides/trump-ai-executive-orders-eo-14179-eo-14365)). The July 2025 US AI Action Plan focuses on boosting data center capacity and exporting American AI technology rather than imposing provider obligations (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52026SC0502)). Predecessor policy—the Biden 2023 Executive Order—targeted "dual-use foundation models," which one legal analysis describes as analogous to the AI Act's "very capable foundation models" (medium confidence) ([DLA Piper](https://knowledge.dlapiper.com/dlapiperknowledge/globalemploymentlatestdevelopments/2023/comparing-the-US-AI-Executive-Order-and-the-EU-AI-Act.html)), but it mainly directed federal agencies rather than imposing direct obligations on private developers, aside from Defense Production Act reporting requirements (medium confidence) ([Brookings](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/regulating-general-purpose-ai-areas-of-convergence-and-divergence-across-the-eu-and-the-us)).

### Comparative Governance Model
EU AI policy is significantly more cautious than current US federal policy, though some US states maintain stricter rules absent federal mandates (medium confidence) ([ESPAS](https://espas.secure.europarl.europa.eu/orbis/system/files/generated/document/en/Near-term-Future-Transatlantic-Relationship-FINAL.pdf)). The voluntary NIST AI RMF—organized around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions—contrasts with the AI Act's binding obligations (low confidence) ([Trustible](https://trustible.ai/ai-governance-frameworks-nist-ai-rmf-eu-ai-act-iso-42001-compared)); firms operating across both markets often use NIST RMF internally to support EU compliance without it substituting for legal duties (low confidence) ([Modulos](https://docs.modulos.ai/frameworks/comparison/nist-ai-rmf-vs-eu-ai-act)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources disagree on whether the AI Act was substantively "updated" in 2025 or merely reinterpreted through guidance, since one source cites only the June 2024 adoption date while another references a 2025 update ([EDPB](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2025-06/spe-training-on-ai-and-data-protection-legal_en.pdf), [ECCouncil](https://www.eccouncil.org/cybersecurity-exchange/responsible-ai-governance/eu-ai-act-nist-ai-rmf-and-iso-iec-42001-a-plain-english-comparison)). Numerous claims regarding enforcement mechanics, fines, timelines, Chapter V structure, and the AI Office's authority carry low confidence (below 0.4) and rely on single, non-official sources, warranting caution.

## Knowledge Gaps
Unclear whether Congress will pass comprehensive federal AI legislation; how EO 14365 interacts with or supersedes Biden-era EO 14110; whether Defense Production Act reporting requirements for dual-use models remain active; what specific provider obligations (if any) the 2025 AI Action Plan imposes; whether US state laws create Article 53-equivalent duties; whether NIST RMF or ISO 42001 are mandatory for federal contractors; and how EU enforcement will apply extraterritorially to US firms absent reciprocal recognition mechanisms.

extracted_claims.text: For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (e.g., biometrics), where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, the provider may choose between internal control conformity assessment (Annex VI, involving the provider's own quality management system) or third-party assessment involving a notified body based on assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation (Annex VII).

For high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products, or are themselves products, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, Section A, the provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure required under that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies also verifying compliance with the AI Act's specific requirements.

Annex VII conformity assessment (notified body route) is treated by industry sources as mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical infrastructure AI, while most other high-risk AI systems may use the Annex VI self-assessment route.

Under Article 43, for the conformity assessment procedure referred to in Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority shall act as the notified body.
A new conformity assessment is required if a high-risk AI system is substantially modified, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, to authorise placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems for exceptional reasons of public security, life/health protection, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets, for a limited period.

Article 43(5) gives the European Commission power to adopt delegated acts (per Article 97) to update Annex VI (internal control procedure) and Annex VII (QMS and technical documentation assessment) in light of technical progress.

# Conformity Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act: Procedures and Notified Body Designation Status

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems—internal control (Annex VI) and third-party assessment via notified bodies (Annex VII)—with the applicable route depending on the AI system's category and whether harmonised standards exist (low confidence). A small number of non-official industry blog sources suggest that, as of March–April 2026, no notified bodies had yet been formally designated specifically under the AI Act; however, this rests on limited, single-source, low-confidence evidence rather than authoritative confirmation, and should be treated as a preliminary signal rather than a settled fact ahead of the August 2026 deadline.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (such as biometrics), where harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, providers may choose between the Annex VI internal control procedure (based on the provider's own quality management system) or third-party assessment under Annex VII involving a notified body's review of the quality management system and technical documentation (low confidence) [Futurium EU AI Approach](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment). Some industry commentary suggests the Annex VII notified-body route is effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems, while other high-risk categories typically rely on Annex VI self-assessment, though this interpretation carries low confidence [Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment), [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems).

For high-risk AI systems that are safety components of, or are themselves, products covered by Union harmonisation legislation (Annex I, Section A), providers must follow the sectoral conformity assessment procedure, with notified bodies also verifying AI Act-specific requirements (high confidence) [AI Act Service Desk, Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai).

Under Article 43, providers may generally choose any notified body for Annex VII assessments, except where the system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions/bodies/agencies—in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk, Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43). A new conformity assessment is required after substantial modification of a high-risk system, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue learning post-deployment (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk, Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard procedures and authorise market placement for exceptional public security, health, environmental, or infrastructural reasons, for a limited period (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk, Article 46](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46). Annex VII, point 4.5, allows notified bodies, upon reasoned request and after exhausting other means, to access training and trained models to assess compliance with Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, subject to IP law (medium confidence) [AI Act Service Desk, Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7). The Commission may also adopt delegated acts to update Annexes VI and VII in light of technical progress (low confidence) [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf).

### Notified Body Designation Infrastructure and Status
The Commission maintains the NANDO information system for publishing lists of designated notified bodies across EU legislation, filterable by legal instrument (high confidence) [EUR-Lex MDR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02017R0745-20260101), [EC Health](https://health.ec.europa.eu/medical-devices-topics-interest/notified-bodies-medical-devices_en). As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 notified bodies under MDR and 19 under IVDR—but these are unrelated to AI Act designations (high confidence) [EUR-Lex SWD](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051). A Council document proposes Annex I.A codes defining AI system categories for notified body designation under Article 30 (medium confidence) [Council ST-7322-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf), and a related proposal, COM(2025) 836, would create a new NANDO Annex XIV and integrate AI Act requirements into aviation safety rules (medium confidence) [Council ST-15708-2025](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf).

Two industry blogs — neither an official EU source — report that, as of March and April 2026 respectively, no AI Act-specific notified bodies had yet appeared to be designated, with designation processes described as ongoing and capacity uncertain; given this rests on a single low-confidence source per claim, it should be read as a tentative signal rather than confirmed fact (low confidence) [eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [AIACT Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide). High-risk obligations, including conformity assessment, are stated by industry sources to fully apply from August 2, 2026, though this too draws on lower-authority sources (low confidence) [Sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026). For comparison, the Cyber Resilience Act faced similar reported delays, with zero notified bodies designated as of late June 2026 despite its own June 2026 rule applicability date, again per a single low-confidence source (low confidence) [CyberCertLabs](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources describing zero designations in March 2026 versus April 2026 are corroborating rather than contradictory, differing only in snapshot date; both are single-source, **low confidence** claims from industry blogs, not official EU confirmation. A more substantive, unresolved tension exists between the August 2026 legal deadline for high-risk obligations and these low-confidence reports of no designated notified bodies as of early-to-mid 2026 — no source reconciles this gap, and no official EU source corroborates the designation-status claims. Multiple claims regarding designation timelines, delegated act powers, and Article 35 administrative rules are rated **low confidence** due to limited source authority or corroboration.

## Knowledge Gaps
No official EU source confirms whether any AI Act notified body has been designated to date; the available evidence pointing to zero designations comes only from industry blogs. The current NANDO listing for AI Act purposes, the finalization status of COM(2025) 836 and the Council's Annex I.A codes, and transitional arrangements bridging the August 2026 deadline with any designation delays remain unclear. Comprehensive mapping of conformity assessment routes across all Annex III categories is also incomplete.

# When Do Annex III High-Risk AI Obligations Under the EU AI Act Start to Apply?

## Executive Summary
As originally adopted in 2024, the EU AI Act set 2 August 2026 as the application date for high-risk AI system obligations, including those in Annex III (high confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/topics/en/article/20230601STO93804/eu-ai-act-first-regulation-on-artificial-intelligence)). However, a subsequent "AI Omnibus" simplification package—politically agreed on 7 May 2026 and entering into force on 27 July 2026—amended this timeline, pushing the application date for Annex III obligations to **2 December 2027** (high confidence) ([EC Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ai-omnibus-enters-force); [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-ai-act-go-effect-what-its-timeline-implementation)). Several sources, particularly those predating the Omnibus amendment, still cite the original 2 August 2026 date, creating a notable discrepancy that researchers should treat with caution.

## Key Findings

### Original Timeline (2024 Act as Adopted)
Under the AI Act as adopted in 2024, obligations for high-risk AI systems—including those enumerated in Annex III—were scheduled to become applicable 36 months after entry into force, corresponding to 2 August 2026 (high confidence) ([European Parliament](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/topics/en/article/20230601STO93804/eu-ai-act-first-regulation-on-artificial-intelligence); [Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20); [Goodwin Law](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2024/10/insights-technology-aiml-eu-ai-act-implementation-timeline)).

### The AI Omnibus Amendment
The EU's "AI Omnibus" (Digital Omnibus on AI) simplification proposal was adopted on 19 November 2025, followed by a political agreement between the Council and Parliament on 7 May 2026, with the resulting amending Regulation entering into force on 27 July 2026 (high confidence) ([EC Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai); [Council of the EU](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/05/07/artificial-intelligence-council-and-parliament-agree-to-simplify-and-streamline-rules)). This amendment is identified in some sources as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, though this citation carries low confidence and warrants independent verification ([AnnexOps](https://annexops.com/eu-ai-act-annex-iii-deadline-2027); [EU AI Compass](https://euaicompass.com/timeline.html)).

### Revised Application Date
Following the Omnibus amendments, obligations for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III now apply from **2 December 2027** (high confidence), as confirmed across multiple official EU guidance sources ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-ai-act-go-effect-what-its-timeline-implementation); [EC Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/navigating-ai-act); [AI Act Service Desk Timeline](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/timeline/timeline-implementation-eu-ai-act)). Separately, high-risk AI systems that are safety components of products regulated under existing EU product safety law (covered via Annex I references) will have obligations applying later still, from 2 August 2028 (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-ai-act-go-effect-what-its-timeline-implementation); [EC Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ai-omnibus-enters-force)).

### Rationale and Mechanism for the Delay
The Commission had proposed adjusting the high-risk rules timeline by up to 16 months, tying application to Commission confirmation that necessary standards and conformity assessment tools were available, rather than a fixed calendar date (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2026/05/07/artificial-intelligence-council-and-parliament-agree-to-simplify-and-streamline-rules)). Delays in the availability of harmonised standards were cited as the reason the original 2 August 2026 date was jeopardized, prompting the extension (medium confidence) ([EC Digital Strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/navigating-ai-act)).

### Transitional Provisions
Under Article 111/113 transitional rules, the Regulation applies to operators of high-risk AI systems already placed on the market before the Chapter III application date only if those systems undergo significant design changes afterward (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727); [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-111)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
A core contradiction exists between older or non-updated sources stating 2 August 2026 as the Annex III application date and updated official guidance confirming 2 December 2027 (low confidence for the outdated claim) ([Cloud Security Alliance](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20) vs. [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/faq/when-does-ai-act-go-effect-what-its-timeline-implementation)). Notably, one source dated April 2026 still treats 2 August 2026 as operative, apparently preceding the Omnibus finalization ([Responsible AI Labs](https://responsibleailabs.ai/knowledge-hub/articles/eu-ai-act-august-2026-compliance)). The EUR-Lex consolidated text references "the date of application of Chapter III" generically without a fixed date, while the AI Act Service Desk's Article 111 guidance names 2 August 2026 explicitly—raising ambiguity about whether this guidance has been fully updated (low confidence flag) ([LinkedIn/Oliver Patel](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/oliver-patel_when-will-eu-ai-act-high-risk-ai-compliance-activity-7401984085377830912-RglO)). Some analysts also note a "backstop" risk: absent formal adoption before 2 August 2026, the original date would technically remain in force (low confidence).

## Knowledge Gaps
The exact amended wording of Article 113(c) remains unclear, including whether it sets a fixed 2 December 2027 date or ties application to Commission confirmation of standards availability. It is uncertain whether Article 111 transitional provisions have been formally updated to reference 2 December 2027. Whether sub-categories within Annex III face staggered application dates, and whether the Commission has issued confirming implementing acts on standards readiness, both require further verification. The correct legal citation for the amending Regulation also needs confirmation.
